title: Multi-Currency FX and Settlement in Southeast Asia: A Guide for Regional Finance Teams
summary: Learn how FX and settlement in Southeast Asia works, and how regional finance teams decide when to hold a currency, when to convert, and where to settle it with Xendit. The post Multi-Currency FX and Settlement in Southeast Asia: A Guide for Regional Finance Teams appeared first on Xendit .
body_markdown:
Regional growth changes what your finance team handles every month.


[ASEAN's total trade in goods](https://asean.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/ASEAN-AR-2024_e-pub_web.pdf) reached around


**USD 3.5 trillion in 2024** , close to the bloc's USD 3.8 trillion GDP, with


**intra-ASEAN trade** accounting for


**21.5%** of the regional total.


As your business builds more commercial relationships across the region, revenue and operating costs begin moving between markets and currencies, which puts


**FX** (Foreign Exchange, the conversion of one currency into another)


**and settlement** in Southeast Asia on your finance team's agenda well before treasury becomes a formal function.


Collecting revenue is one part of that work. As your business expands globally, a second set of demands appears, particularly the need to receive and send funds across


**multiple currencies** **and markets** . Money has to reach suppliers, channel partners, other entities in your group, and customers waiting on refunds, and each of those obligations can fall in a currency other than the one you collected.


Liquidity has moved up the agenda at the same time. Deloitte's


[2026 Asia Pacific CFO Pulse Survey](https://www.deloitte.com/southeast-asia/en/about/press-room/southeast-asia-cfos-confidence-global-uncertainty.html) found


**55%** of Southeast Asia CFOs increasing their focus on


**liquidity** and


**cash management** , while


**42%** are prioritizing greater


**operational efficiency** . For a business collecting revenue and funding operations across several markets, that priority turns into a specific operational question, which is what to do with each amount once it has been collected.


FX and settlement decisions cover three things once the money has been collected, namely which currency to keep it in, when to convert it, and where the funds finally arrive. Those three choices determine how much of your regional cash is available where you need it, how much you lose to conversion costs, and how much time your team spends closing the books each month. Handled without a clear rule, they erode margin quietly and make cash positions harder to forecast.


**Key takeaways:**


- Why FX and settlement get harder as operations spread across more Southeast Asian markets


- What fragmented currency handling costs in conversion fees, visibility, and reconciliation time


- How to decide whether to hold, convert, or settle each incoming currency


- What to look for in multi-currency settlement infrastructure


- How Xendit supports currency balances, conversion, and cross-border settlement from one dashboard


The strain rarely appears in your first market. It builds as your business adds countries, entities, and payment obligations that no longer share a single currency.


## **Why FX and settlement get harder as your regional operations scale**


Operating in more markets means your business can


**collect, hold, convert, and settle several currencies** at the same time. The difficulty comes from keeping track of where funds are, what conversion has already taken place, and what amount finally reaches the business, and each of those gets harder with every market you add.


Four


**operational pressures** explain why FX and settlement management becomes harder for businesses running across multiple Southeast Asian markets:


### **1. Currency flows fragment market by market**


A regional business can collect customer payments in one currency, report financially in another, and need funds for operations in a third.


Without a


**centralized setup** , your team ends up managing separate bank accounts, payment providers, and currency balances country by country. That setup makes it slow to confirm how much liquidity your business holds across the region and which markets hold it, which delays every decision about moving funds.


***Also read:***[Scaling E-Commerce Payments Across Southeast Asia: Why Businesses Need Cross-Border Payment Infrastructure](https://www.xendit.co/en/blog/scaling-e-commerce-payments-across-southeast-asia-why-businesses-need-cross-border-payment-infrastructure/)


### **2. Every conversion becomes another financial event to track**


When the payment currency differs from the currency your business ultimately needs, the conversion itself becomes a transaction your team has to account for.


Even one customer payment then produces several records your team has to match against each other:


- The original transaction amount and currency


- The amount converted


- The FX rate applied


- The settlement currency


- The final amount received


Converting the same funds twice doubles both the record-keeping and the cost. Funds moved into a central currency and later moved back to cover an obligation in the original market pass through two conversions and two sets of fees. For your business, catching this pattern early prevents a cost that repeats every time the same flow runs.


### **3. Settlement extends beyond the choice of currency** ****


Choosing a currency and choosing a settlement destination are two different decisions. Your team also has to work out which country and which account the funds need to reach.


Depending on the business flow,


**funds may need to** :


- Stay in the same currency and the same market


- Move to another country without changing currency


- Move cross-border and convert into another currency


FX and settlement therefore become tied to where the business actually needs liquidity, which puts the decision with whoever has visibility into upcoming obligations in each market.


### **4. Limited FX visibility creates uncertainty about the final amount**


Cross-border payments can involve different fees, conversion rates, settlement timelines, and intermediary steps. Without


**clear visibility** into each of those, your team may struggle to explain why the final amount received differs from the amount originally collected. That gap adds reconciliation work and makes regional cash positions harder to forecast.


******


These four pressures share the same root, which is the distance between where funds are collect


ed and where your business can see or use them. That distance carries a price, and it appears in places your finance team can measure.


***Also read:***[Cross-Border Payments Feel Too Complex? Here's How to Simplify Them](https://www.xendit.co/en-id/blog/cross-border-payments-feel-too-complex-heres-how-to-simplify-them/)


## **What fragmented FX and settlement operations cost your finance team**


As transaction volume and market count grow, managing currency separately in every market tends to produce a familiar set of outcomes.


Here is what


**fragmented FX and settlement operations typically cost** a regional finance team:


- Higher or repeated currency-conversion charges


- More manual work tracing original amounts through to settled amounts


- Limited visibility into regional liquidity


- Funds held in currencies or markets where they are not currently needed


- Slower reconciliation and cash-flow forecasting


- Continued uncertainty over the final amount received after FX and settlement


The underlying issue is control, because managing several currencies is workable on its own, and what gets harder with every market you add is keeping control over where funds are held, when conversion happens, and where they finally settle.


Making that control practical starts with a decision your team can apply to each incoming currency.


## **Hold, convert, or settle: How to decide what happens to each incoming currency**


When every incoming currency gets the same treatment, the system decides for you. Your team can instead start from what the business will need those funds for next.


Currency mismatch affects the accounts directly, and it shows up in


[three forms](https://www.jpmorgan.com/insights/treasury/liquidity-management/fx-exposure-netting-risk-management-solutions) that regional businesses run into regularly:


- **Funding mismatch** , where a company borrows in one currency and earns revenue in another


- **Revenue and expense mismatch** , where collections and payables fall in different currencies


- **Intercompany transactions** , where cross-currency invoices move between group companies


For a regional business in Southeast Asia, the second and third turn up in day-to-day operations, since local revenue and local costs rarely line up exactly and entities in different markets bill one another.


Internal flows make up more of that activity than most teams expect, with


[up to 30% of a firm's transactional activity](https://www.jpmorgan.com/insights/treasury/liquidity-management/fx-exposure-netting-risk-management-solutions) taking place between related parties. For your business, that share is significant because intercompany fund movement is the part you control directly, which makes it the first place to look for conversions your business could avoid.


**Timing** carries a consequence as well. When


**exchange rates** move between the point a transaction is initiated and the point it settles, the resulting realized FX gains or losses are reported in the income statement. Conversion timing therefore reaches your profit and loss, so your team should decide when it happens instead of letting a default setting decide.


With that in mind, each


**incoming amount can be assigned** to one of three treatments:


### **1. Hold the currency when you have obligations in that market**


If revenue collected in a market will later fund expenses, supplier payments, partner settlements, payroll, refunds, or other payouts in the same currency, keeping some of those funds locally removes the need to convert twice.


This works best when your team has visibility into upcoming obligations by market, so the balance you hold reflects a forecast.


### **2. Convert when the funds are needed in another currency**


Conversion earns its cost when local revenue needs to be consolidated into your reporting, treasury, or operating currency, particularly where few obligations remain in the original currency.


What your team needs at that moment is visibility into the applicable rate, the fees or spread, and the resulting converted amount before the conversion is committed.


### **3. Settle across borders when another entity or market needs the funds**


Sometimes the requirement goes beyond conversion, because the money has to move to another country or another legal entity.


A regional business may collect locally in one market while the funds are needed at headquarters, at a second operating entity, or by a supplier based elsewhere in the region. The settlement path then has to match the destination, and the destination is set by the obligation.


When applied consistently, these three treatments turn currency handling into a repeatable rule your team can document. Holding to that rule depends on what your systems allow.


## **Six capabilities to look for in multi-currency settlement infrastructure**


Once your business operates across several currencies, the hold, convert, or settle rule only holds up if your systems can carry it out. That means more control over where funds are held, when conversion happens, and where money finally settles.


These are the


**capabilities** that determine whether your finance team can execute those decisions across daily collections, conversions, and settlements:


### **1. Consolidated visibility across currency balances**


Your team needs to be able to see funds across currencies from one place instead of checking separate accounts and portals market by market. Without it, the hold-or-convert decision gets made on incomplete information.


### **2. Flexibility over when FX happens**


Where operationally and legally available, your business should be able to keep a matching currency balance in place of converting every payment on arrival. That flexibility is what makes holding a currency a real option.


### **3. Transparent conversion information**


Before a conversion is executed, your team needs the source currency, destination currency, applicable rate, fees or spread, and resulting amount. When your team can review and accept the rate first, the converted amount is known upfront instead of discovered during the next reconciliation.


### **4. Flexible settlement destinations**


The setup should support the range of money flows your business actually runs, from keeping funds inside the local market to moving them cross-border in the same or a different currency.


### **5. Connectivity between collections and payouts**


Regional treasury gets more efficient when money collected in local markets can fund subsequent business payments, so collections, FX, and payouts stop running as three disconnected processes.


### **6. Consistent records for reconciliation**


Your team needs a clear trail connecting collection, currency balance, conversion, and settlement or payout, so your finance and audit teams can explain how the amount a customer paid became the amount that arrived in another market.


Building these capabilities out of separate banks and payment providers is where most regional finance teams lose time. Running them from one account is what changes the workload.

## **FAQ for regional finance teams in Southeast Asia: FX, currency balances, and settlement**


### **Can you hold a currency balance instead of converting every payment on arrival?**


Yes, where that currency balance is available to your account.


**Xendit** converts payments into your account's default currency, which is USD for global accounts, until you


[open a balance in another currency](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/balance-overview) . Once that balance is open, payments with a matching presentment currency settle into it without conversion, so your business can keep local funds available for local obligations.


### **Which currencies should your business hold instead of converting?**


Start from your upcoming obligations in each market, including supplier payments, payroll, partner settlements, and refunds, since a currency you will spend locally is one worth holding locally. Currencies with few local obligations are the better candidates for conversion into your treasury or operating currency. With


**Xendit** ,


[balances](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/balance-overview) are opened selectively per currency, so your setup follows those obligations instead of converting everything by default.


### **Can you settle funds into a bank account in a different country from where the payment was made?**


The path depends on whether the currency changes along the way.


**Xendit** supports


[same-currency local withdrawals, same-currency cross border withdrawals, and different-currency cross border withdrawals](https://help.xendit.co/hc/en-us/articles/49495514836633-How-does-multi-currency-settlement-work-for-withdrawal) , so funds can stay in the market, move country without conversion, or move and convert in one step. Your team selects the option that matches where the liquidity is needed.


### **How do you see the FX rate before a conversion goes through?**


The rate is quoted before you confirm. In the


**Xendit** dashboard,


[converting between balances](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/convert-balance) shows the rate for that currency pair and the amount you will receive, with the quote refreshing every 30 seconds and a PIN required to confirm. Teams automating this can request a rate through the


[Foreign Exchange API](https://docs.xendit.co/apidocs/foreign-exchange-introduction) and act on it within the window it stays active.


### **How do you trace the amount you received back to the payment the customer made?**


You need the original amount and currency, the converted amount, the rate applied, the settlement currency, and the final amount received, all held in one record.


[Xendit Transactions Report](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/transactions-report) carries those fields on the same line, including the Forex Rate and Settlement Currency, so your finance team can follow the chain without matching exports from several providers by hand.


### **Do you need a separate bank account in every market to run multi-currency operations?**


Opening an account per market is one route, and it usually leaves your team reconciling across separate portals, providers, and reporting formats.


**Xendit** consolidates receiving, holding, converting, and


[paying out](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/send-payouts-overview) across currencies within one account, which reduces how much your operating model depends on country-by-country banking relationships as you add markets.


### **How can you reduce the cost of converting between currencies across your regional operations?**


Two variables drive the cost, which are how often you convert and the rate you convert at. Holding matching currency balances removes conversions your business never needed, and


[Xendit Cross Border](https://www.xendit.co/en/products/cross-border-payments/) applies wholesale rates with the option to confirm the rate online before a transfer, so your team can see the converted amount before the transfer goes through.
